A Year in the Life of Marijuana Prohibition -- 1998
A Chronology By Kevin Nelson

April 12, 1999

By Kevin Nelson, kcnelson@premier1.net,
Member of the Bellingham Washington Drug Policy Reform Group.

"One of the problems that the marijuana reform movement consistently faces is that everyone wants to talk about what marijuana does, but no one ever wants to look at what marijuana prohibition does. Marijuana never kicks down your door in the middle of the night. Marijuana never locks up sick and dying people, does not suppress medical research, does not peek in bedroom windows. Even if one takes every reefer madness allegation of the prohibitionists at face value, marijuana prohibition has done far more harm to far more people than marijuana ever could." –Richard Cowan, former head of NORML, as quoted By William F. Buckley, Jr.

January

1/15/98 Georgia Senator Ralph David Abernathy III, the son of civil rights leader Ralph Abernathy, is censured by the Georgia State ethics committee for trying to smuggle 3.4 grams (1/8 ounce) of marijuana from Jamaica.

1/22/98 A Missouri judge sentences Billy Polson, 17, an adolescent first-time offender to 10 years in state prison after finding him guilty of selling $20 of marijuana (3.4 grams) to undercover informant Alex Martinez, within 2,000 feet of Central Methodist College. Martinez- who dated Polson’s sister at the time- admitted purchasing malt liquor for the underage defendant shortly before Polson agreed to sell him marijuana.

1/25/98 Sir Paul McCartney, revealed in an interview with London’s Independent on Sunday, how he broke the news of the influence of marijuana to the Beatles’ producer, Sir George Martin. "When George asked me, ‘do you know what caused (Sgt.) Pepper?’ I said, ‘in one word - pot’." Martin refused to believe him saying, "But you weren’t on it all the time." Sir Paul replied: "Yes, we were."

February

2/11/98 Canadian snowboarder Ross Rebagliati, 26, is briefly stripped of the first-ever Olympic gold medal for giant slalom snowboarding, after testing positive for marijuana immediately following his race.

2/19/98 Britain’s prestigious journal, New Scientist, formally opines against marijuana prohibition: "

2/27/98 Canadian Health Minister Allan Rock announces that cultivation of industrial hemp (marijuana’s non-psychoactive cousin) will be legal nationwide by mid-March.

March

3/14/98 Canada’s largest newspaper The Globe and Mail reports that Canadians are being barred indefinitely from entering America when they respond affirmatively to US Border agents’ question: "Have you ever smoked marijuana in your lifetime?" [If Canadian border guards employed this tactic, they would bar Bill Clinton, Al and Tipper Gore, Newt Gingrich, Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas, and 65+ million other Americans from entering.]

3/20/98 In California, Myron Mower, a blind man with terminal degenerative diabetes, and subject to otherwise uncontrollable fits of vomiting, is convicted of felony cultivation of 31 marijuana plants in his garden, despite Proposition 215. He is sentenced to pay $1,000 in fines and submit to random house searches and drug tests for 5 years.

3/20/98 Former L.A. Lakers center Kareem Abdul-Jabbar is fined $500 for trying to pass through Toronto/into U.S. Customs with 6 grams of marijuana.

3/25/98 Peter Baez, cancer patient, cousin of folk-singer Joan Baez, and Director of the San Jose Cannabis Buyer’s Club is arrested for selling marijuana to Enrique Robles. Robles suffers from complications of a broken back, but prosecutors said his doctor did not formally recommend marijuana.

3/28/98 Sixteen thousand Brits march on Trafalgar Square to legalize marijuana. It is the largest event of its kind in 30 years.

April

4/10/98 According to ESPN, offensive tackle Tra Thomas and tight end Alonzo Mayes, a pair of projected first-round picks in next weekend’s NFL draft, test positive for marijuana. Mayes was an All Big-12 selection and consensus All-American with Oklahoma State last season.

4/11/98 California cancer patient Todd McCormick, awaiting trial for growing marijuana for himself and other patients, is processed into a federal prison: "strip-searched and given prison uniforms in a room with a leaking sewage pipe. The floor, on which McCormick had to walk barefoot, was covered with human urine and excrement. McCormick was not allowed to bring the special orthopedic pillow he uses to support his head—his top five vertebra were fused together during cancer treatment when he was two years old. Inside federal prison, he was told that there were "no more pillows," not of any kind… the prison is kept inhumanly cold 24 hours a day."

4/13/98 Charlotte Hornets guard Vernon Maxwell begins a 90-day prison sentence for possession of 1 gram ($10) of marijuana. [Maxwell will lose approximately $100,000 in salary during this time, of which the US government will lose approximately $25,000 in lost tax revenues, plus the additional $5,000 cost to incarcerate Maxwell.]

4/13/98 The New York Times formally opines in favor of hemp cultivation in America. "The marketplace, not myopic rules, should determine hemp’s future in America."

4/28/98 Congress passes a bill to deny student financial aid to anyone convicted of marijuana possession. No such law exists to similarly punish convicted rapists or other violent offenders.

4/ 28/98 In Crown Point, Indiana, the Lake County Sheriff’s Department arrests a Times reporter Friday who has been investigating allegations of corruption and mismanagement in the Lake County Drug Task Force. Two detectives from the sheriff’s internal affairs division arrested Times staff writer Daniel J. Yovich about 1:30 p.m. at The Times’ Munster office.

Several months prior, Yovich was subjected to a search by sheriff’s deputies.

Friday’s arrest, which followed a series of stories Yovich recently wrote detailing allegations of corruption and misappropriation of resources at the drug task force, was for two misdemeanor warrants dating back as far as 1993. Sheriff John Buncich’s public relations chief issued a tersely worded statement that blamed the possible loss of millions of dollars in drug task force grants on The Times, an apparent reference to Yovich’s stories. "I have been advised that congressional funding may not be renewed because of negative reporting by The Times," the written statement said. "I, as your sheriff, along with other police chiefs throughout Lake County, will not permit this to happen."

May

5/14/98 Brian Taylor, the Mayor of Grand Forks, BC, is barred from entering the United States for being a "drug trafficker." Taylor had grown industrial hemp without government approval.

June

6/4/98 Bob Denver, star of "Gilligan’s Island," is arrested at his home for receiving one ounce of marijuana through the mail.

6/5/98 Attorney General Janet Reno declares her support of Oregon’s assisted-suicide law, concluding that "federal law does not authorize the prosecution of a physician who complies with the Oregon law." [However, Reno continues to harass doctors who prescribe medical marijuana in an effort to save patient’s lives, despite state medical marijuana laws.]

6/5/98 In U.S. Army tests, rats injected with Dexanabinol, a marijuana derivative, were more than 70 percent less likely to suffer epileptic seizures or brain damage after exposure to sarin and other nerve gases, according to results published in the Israeli press in Jerusalem.

6/8/98 A petition calling for an end to America’s Drug War is presented to the United Nations General Assembly. Among the 500 signatories included are former heads of state, former UN Secretary General Javier Perez de Cuellar, and America’s most trusted journalist Walter Cronkite. U.S. Drug Czar Barry McCaffrey dismisses petition signatories as members of the "intellectual, literary and academic community engaging in pseudo-science."

6/29/98 The Ottowa Citizen’s editorial board calls U.S. Drug Czar ‘gonzo.’ "General McCaffrey’s bitter, paranoid attacks, coming as they did hard upon the UN conference on drugs and the debate about drug prohibition that it prompted, exposed just how empty the drug warriors’ case really is. Bereft of evidence, belied by experience, drug prohibitionists have few rational arguments to make—so they insult, vilify, and denounce."

July

7/4/98 British-born biologist Aidan Hampson, at the US National Institute for Mental Health, in Maryland, reports that two active components of marijuana - THC and cannabidiol - will each act to prevent damage to brain tissue in stroke patients and possibly Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s patients. [While the BBC News and the Manchester Guardian cover the story, no American newspaper picks it up.]

7/14/98 Drug Czar Barry McCaffrey begins a tour of Europe with an inflammatory speech in Stockholm, Sweden, attacking the Netherlands "harm reduction" drug policy. "The murder rate in Holland is double that in the United States. The per capita crime rates are much higher than the United States… That’s drugs." McCaffrey said the United States had 8.22 murders per 100,000 people in 1995 compared to 17.58 in The Netherlands. [Oops! The actual Dutch murder rate is approximately 1.3 murders per 100,000, or less than 20% of the US rate. No American newspaper challenges the inaccuracy.]

7/17/98 Former San Bernadino County Sheriff David Herrick is sentenced to four years in prison for selling medical marijuana through the Orange County Cannabis Buyer’s Co-op. Herrick began using marijuana for chronic pain after he was run over by a car and was forced to leave his sheriff’s position.

7/20/98 CBS Sportsline reports that an estimated 70 per cent of all NBA players smoke marijuana.

7/23/98 Peter McWilliams, an AIDS and cancer patient, and a self-publisher whose books include "How to Survive the Loss of a Love," "How to Heal Depression," and the "Life 101" series, is indicted for "conspiring to grow marijuana" for patients in Southern California. He contends he uses marijuana to ease the nausea caused by the AIDS drugs he takes to sustain his life.

7/30/98 Oklahoma takes state custody of newborn infant immediately after birth when the mother tests positive for marijuana.

August

8/2/98 U.S. prison population surges to record 1.25 million people. America is "Number One" with highest percentage of its own population in jail.

8/13/98 Following months of police pressure, the West Australian Government announces a reduced cautioning system for first-time cannabis offenders caught with small quantities of the drug for personal use. "It’s good to see that at last the Government has recognised the merit of our argument that precious police and court resources should not be wasted on minor cannabis users."

8/19/98 Saying a 93-year prison term for medical marijuana cultivation "shocks our conscience," a Tulsa County appeals court reduces Oklahoman Will Foster’s punishment to a 20-year sentence.

September

9/5/98 Dreadlocked African-American George Singleton is arrested in Oklahoma during a cross-country business trip. He is initially charged with carrying an "imitation controlled substance" (mullein and rosemary), and is held for 25 days in jail. Despite a negative blood test for intoxicating substances, he is charged with DUI. Craig Co., OK, DA Gene Haynes acknowledged, "It is an unusual case because of the fact that we don’t have proof of any illegal substance." But he told the Tulsa World, "We’re continuing to pursue it because we feel he was under some type of influence that rendered him a danger on the roadway."

9/15/98 Congress passes Resolution 117, stating that "marijuana is a dangerous and addictive drug and should not be legalized for medical use."

9/22/98 The Seattle Times carries a scathing attack on opponents of medical marijuana: "(WA Lt. Gov. Brad) Owen casually dismisses real stories of those who have benefited from medical marijuana as "anecdotal evidence." On Nov. 3, the flesh-and-blood family, friends and co-workers of those "anecdotes" can wrest control from calculating bureaucrats like Owen and put the power to heal - with dignity, privacy, and freedom from fear - in the frail fingers of their loved ones."

October

10/5/98 Amnesty International, in its first campaign directed at any Western nation, publishes a harsh report on the United States, saying U.S. police forces and criminal and legal systems have "a persistent and widespread pattern of human rights violations."

10/7/98 Pharmos Corporation (Nasdaq: PARS) presents the results of a successful Phase II clinical study with Dexanabinol, a non-psychotropic synthetic analog of marijuana, in the treatment of severe head trauma patients. No drug is currently approved to treat severe head trauma, the leading cause of death among children and young adults in the U.S.

10/8/98 A pamphlet by Gerald Smith, a criminology professor in Utah, and endorsed by Sen. Orrin Hatch vividly describes these warning signs for the benefit of parents worried that their children may be regular users of marijuana and other drugs. The affected youth may show "excessive preoccupation with social causes, race relations, environmental issues, etc".

10/14/98 DEA eradication figures suggest domestic marijuana production ranks as the fourth largest cash crop in America. It is the Number One revenue-producing crop in 10 states.

10/24/98 Congress prevents the DC Board of Elections from using public funds to count and certify the results of the Nov. 4th medical marijuana initiative vote. Estimated cost: $1.64. [This is perhaps the first occasion in American history when the federal government has moved to censor the results of a free and legal domestic election. Democracy is annulled.]

November

11/4/98 Voters in Oregon, Nevada, Washington, Colorado, Alaska, Arizona, and the District of Columbia vote to legalize the use of marijuana for medical purposes. Exit polls in DC report 69-31 voting in favor of the initiative.

11/11/98 Britain’s House of Lords’ Science and Technology Committee calls for medical cannabis trials "as a matter of urgency for compassionate reasons" as thousands of patients could be helped. "It would be unjustified and inhumane to make them wait much longer."

11/14/98 The premier British medical journal, The Lancet, pronounces that "moderate indulgence in cannabis has little ill-effect on health, and that decisions to ban or legalise cannabis should be based on other considerations." The editors added, "It would be reasonable to judge cannabis less of a threat to health than alcohol or tobacco."

11/30/98 Germany’s drug czar, Christa Nickels, asks for a debate on the acceptance of cannabis for use as a medicine: "The suffering of patients with illnesses such as MS, Cancer or AIDS could be eased with cannabis," she said.

December

12/8/98 Michigan Circuit Judge William Cahalan rules that businessman Alfred Martin, who has led "an exemplary life" since being convicted of selling $10 worth of marijuana 25 years ago, should be extradited to Virginia, where he walked off a prison farm for his marijuana conviction. Martin is led away from family and friends to begin a 10-year prison sentence. "It’s all the more difficult when you see the family here and understand that the family is a credit to the state and Mr. Martin has been a credit to the state for the past 25 years," Judge Cahalan said.

12/9/98 150 angry Belpre, OH, residents show up at a community forum to protest the killing of Delbert Bonar, 57, a retired school custodian. The surprise nighttime police raid in search of marijuana caused Mr. Bonar to awake from sleep and grab an unloaded shotgun to confront the intruders. He was shot 8 times. Two ounces of marijuana were recovered from the house. [A fabulous drug war victory!]

12/18/98 The Chicago Tribune reports that recent research indicates that the human body is teeming with marijuana-like compounds called cannabinoids. "Discovered in humans just a few years ago and, until recently, virtually unstudied, the compounds have become one of the looming mysteries of the nervous system, and a field of exploding scientific interest… In 1992, an Israeli pharmacology team led by Raphael Mechoulam and William Devane discovered that humans produced their own cannabinoids. They called the substance anandamide (Sanskrit for "eternal bliss")… Animal studies show cannabinoids can block other kinds of pain almost before they begin, stopping the pain signals before they reach the spinal cord or brain, working as well as morphine. That power suggests they could be substituted for morphine, which is addictive and must be used in increasing doses over time… Cannabinoids also counteract nausea, another plus for patients with cancer and AIDS."

12/30/98 Despite Washington State’s recently-passed medical marijuana initiative, Tracie Morgan, 61, and her blind son who has AIDS, Kelly Grubbs, 35, are arrested after Tacoma police find three marijuana plants in their home. Grubbs was diagnosed with an advanced stage of AIDS in 1996. Since then, according to his mother, he has had a stroke, lost his eyesight and is semi-paralyzed on one side of his body. But medications have caused a recent rebound, she said, and marijuana is playing a role in improving Grubbs’ eyesight. Police contend they acted properly because Grubbs and Morgan had no medical documents showing they were authorized to grow marijuana for personal medical use. The Pierce County DA later dismissed the case.

The year-end tallies:

Deaths attributed to tobacco: 440,000

Deaths attributed to alcohol: +/- 125,000

Deaths attributed to legal prescription drugs: 106,000

Deaths attributed to illegal drugs: 14,000

Deaths attributed to marijuana: 0

Marijuana arrests in 1998: 695,000 [A new record! One arrest every 45 seconds]

Total number of marijuana arrests under the Clinton administration, so far: 2,800,000
